title: Emoor Bhagavathy Devaswom vs M S Hill Top Plantations
court: High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam
summary: The Kerala High Court held that the appellants are not entitled to fixity of tenure under Section 13(1) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, nor are they deemed tenants under Sections 6A and 7D of the Act. Ext.B3 lease deed was held to be a void document as it is hit by Section 74 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, thereby disentitling the appellants to claim compensation for value of improvements. All regular second appeals were dismissed and cross-objections were allowed, restoring the judgment and decree of the trial court granting recovery of possession.

summary: The applicant, a non-banking financial institution, filed an application under Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, seeking appointment of an Advocate Commissioner/Receiver to repossess a vehicle (Motor Car Chassis No.MA3TFC62SPA212133, Engine No.K10CN1103784, Registration No.TN19W8281) due to default in loan repayment (12 installments in arrears, amounting to Rs.1,41,600/-). The Court initially appointed an Advocate Commissioner on 30.06.2025 with directions for repayment terms and initiation of arbitration within 90 days. Upon noting that private notice to the respondents returned with a 'refused' endorsement (deemed service), and noting that the initial remuneration had been paid, the Court appointed Mr. Vasantha Rooban Abishek I.J., Legal Executive, as Receiver to seize the subject vehicle with police aid if required.

sourceDerivedSummary: The High Court erred in limiting the actions of the accused to mere 'preparation' rather than 'attempt' to commit rape under criminal jurisprudence. Third-party witness intervention prevented the further commission of the crime, which constitutes an overt act beyond preparation.
aiAnalysis: AI Analysis: This judgment highlights the Supreme Court's proactive intervention not only in correcting erroneous lower court interpretations regarding the threshold between 'preparation' and 'attempt' in heinous sexual offenses against minors but also instituting structural administrative measures via an expert committee to address judicial insensitivity.

summary: This civil appeal addressed the limitation period and the applicability of Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, to appeals filed under Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, read with Section 13(1A) of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015. relatedAuthority.caseTitle: Kanwar Singh Saini v. High Court of Delhi

notes: Key legal argument: Execution of interim order after final dismissal is an abuse of process.

evidence.issueTitle: Merger of Interim Order into Final Judgment
evidence.claim: Arrears accrued under an interim maintenance order during pendency represent a vested statutory debt enforceable despite subsequent dismissal.
evidence.evidenceExcerpt: Respondent contended that maintenance rights crystalized during the period between interim order dated 06.07.2017 and final dismissal on 16.01.2018 represent legally enforceable debt under Section 125(3).

evidence.issueTitle: Suppression of Income and Employment
evidence.claim: Wife actively suppressed substantial commission income from LIC Agency while claiming inability to maintain herself under Section 125 Cr.P.C.
evidence.evidenceExcerpt: Form 16A and bank statement of Bank of Maharashtra (A/c No. 6003291823) demonstrates regular commission payments of Rs. 38,500/month received from Life Insurance Corporation of India.
notes: Violation of full income disclosure affidavit mandated under Rajnesh v. Neha.

evidence.issueTitle: Suppression of Income and Employment
evidence.claim: Commission income is volatile, non-guaranteed and insufficient to cover spiraling medical expenditures of minor child.
evidence.evidenceExcerpt: Rebuttal affidavit states LIC renewal commissions have dwindled to negligible sums and are irregular; petitioner earns over Rs. 95,000/month as Senior Assistant in Zilla Parishad.
